opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it's been striking, even from the inside. I spend most of my time building evaluations, and one of the clearest signals of the pace is how quickly our evals stop being useful. We'll design something we think is really hard, something that should hold up for a year or two, and within a few months the models are saturating it. So a big part of my job has become constantly asking: what's the next, harder thing we should measure?

What's changed is *what* the progress looks like. A few years ago we were measuring things like multiple-choice exams or short reasoning puzzles. Now the more interesting question is whether models can do real, economically valuable work, the kinds of tasks a lawyer, nurse, engineer, or analyst does over hours or days. When you measure that way, with experts in those fields grading the outputs, you see models getting meaningfully closer to expert quality on a growing share of tasks, and doing it much faster and cheaper.

That said, I try to be careful not to overstate it. There's still a real gap between doing well on a well-scoped task and reliably handling the messy, long-horizon, context-heavy work people do every day. Models still make mistakes a human expert wouldn't, and they don't always know when they're wrong. So my view is that progress is fast and, if anything, accelerating on the dimensions we can measure, and the hardest and most important part is building measurements that keep up, so we actually understand what these systems can and can't do before they're deployed widely.

r001.rationale: The response describes rapid and accelerating progress, but does not say that public awareness underestimates its pace.

r002.rationale: The response does not link Tejal Patwardhan’s conviction about AGI to early access to powerful AI models.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it's faster than I expected, and I work on this every day. The thing that's hard to convey from the outside is how compressed the cycles have become. A capability that felt like a research milestone a year ago is now something we treat as a baseline we build on top of.

I think about it mostly through evaluations, because that's my job. We build evals to measure things models can't do yet, and the shelf life of those evals keeps shrinking. You design a benchmark thinking it'll give you a couple of years of signal, and then a model saturates it in a few months. That's happened enough times now that it's not a surprise anymore, it's a pattern.

The other thing I'd point to is the shift from narrow tasks to long-horizon work. Early on, progress meant getting better at answering a question. Now it means a model can take a vague goal, break it into steps, use tools, recover from mistakes, and come back with something useful after working for a long time. That's a qualitatively different kind of capability, and it's the part that's moving fastest.

So the short answer is: steady, compounding, and not slowing down in any way I can measure. The challenge for people like me is building measurement that keeps pace with that, because if you can't measure it, you can't reason carefully about what it means or how to deploy it safely.

astra-6.text: I think the pace is remarkable, but it’s uneven. You’ll see a model make a big leap in one area and still struggle with something that feels relatively simple. So I’d separate how quickly capabilities are improving from how quickly we can make those capabilities reliable and useful. The exciting part is watching something move from “that’s an interesting demo” to “I can actually use this in my work.”

r001.rationale: The response calls progress remarkable but uneven; it does not say public awareness underestimates its pace.

sol-6.1.text: I think the pace is remarkable, but it’s uneven. A model can make a big leap on a difficult task and still struggle with something that seems straightforward. So I’d distinguish between how quickly capabilities are improving and how quickly we can make those capabilities reliable enough for people to use every day. Both matter. The exciting part is seeing what becomes possible; the hard part is understanding where the limits still are.
